title: Inferior thyroid artery, the recurrent laryngeal nerve and parathyroid blood supply
text:
The inferior thyroid artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk, arches medially behind the carotid sheath and meets the recurrent laryngeal nerve near the lower pole, where the nerve may pass in front of, behind or between its branches. The nerve then enters the larynx just behind the dense suspensory ligament of Berry, the commonest site of injury during lobectomy. The right nerve runs more obliquely; in about 0.5 to 1% it is 'non-recurrent', coming straight off the vagus at the level of the thyroid, always with an aberrant right subclavian artery.
The inferior thyroid artery also supplies both parathyroid glands on that side. Modern thyroidectomy therefore ligates its branches on the capsule of the gland (capsular dissection) rather than tying the main trunk, preserving parathyroid perfusion and reducing post-operative hypocalcaemia. Nerve monitoring and routine identification of the recurrent nerve reduce palsy; bilateral palsy leaves both cords near the midline, causing stridor that may need reintubation or tracheostomy.

title: Thyroid cancer and the central neck compartment
text:
The thyroid drains first to the central compartment (level VI): the prelaryngeal (Delphian) node on the cricothyroid membrane, the pretracheal nodes and the paratracheal nodes along the recurrent laryngeal nerves; then to the lateral deep cervical chain (levels II-IV) and the upper mediastinum (level VII).
Papillary carcinoma, the commonest type (radiation exposure, young women), spreads by lymphatics and often presents as a lateral neck node, yet carries an excellent prognosis. A palpable Delphian node signals aggressive laryngotracheal spread. Follicular carcinoma spreads by the blood to bone and lung and is diagnosed by capsular or vascular invasion, which fine-needle cytology cannot assess. Medullary carcinoma (C cells, calcitonin and CEA as markers, germline RET mutations in MEN2, prophylactic thyroidectomy in carriers) involves central nodes early. Anaplastic carcinoma in the elderly grows rapidly and compresses the trachea. Differentiated cancers take up iodine, so radioiodine ablation after total thyroidectomy treats residual disease and thyroglobulin is used for follow-up.

title: Diabetes insipidus and the posterior pituitary
text:
Antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin are made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and carried down the pituitary stalk to be stored in the neurohypophysis (the 'bright spot' on T1-weighted MRI). Cranial diabetes insipidus results from pituitary or hypothalamic surgery, head injury, craniopharyngioma, germinoma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, sarcoidosis or metastases (breast, lung); nephrogenic DI results from lithium, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia or AVP receptor mutations.
Patients pass large volumes of dilute urine with thirst and a high-normal or high sodium. A water deprivation test shows persisting dilute urine; a rise in urine osmolality after desmopressin confirms the cranial form. After pituitary stalk injury a triphasic response is classic: DI (days 1-5), then SIADH as stored hormone leaks out, then permanent DI if most neurones die. Tumours confined to the anterior pituitary rarely cause DI, so its presence suggests a hypothalamic or stalk lesion.

title: Hypophyseal portal system and the stalk effect
text:
The anterior pituitary has no direct arterial supply of its own for most of its mass: hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones reach it through the hypophyseal portal veins in the stalk. Dopamine from the arcuate nucleus tonically inhibits prolactin secretion, so prolactin is the only anterior pituitary hormone that RISES when the stalk is compressed or cut.
A non-functioning macroadenoma or other sellar mass compressing the stalk causes modest hyperprolactinaemia (the 'stalk effect') with low levels of the other hormones; a very high prolactin indicates a prolactinoma. The distinction matters because prolactinomas, even large ones, shrink with dopamine agonists (cabergoline), whereas non-functioning adenomas need surgery. Antipsychotics and metoclopramide (dopamine antagonists), hypothyroidism (TRH stimulates prolactin) and pregnancy also raise prolactin.
The portal dependence explains why the enlarged anterior pituitary of pregnancy infarcts with postpartum hypotension (Sheehan syndrome), often presenting first as failure of lactation.

title: Transsphenoidal pituitary surgery
text:
Most pituitary tumours are removed endoscopically through the nose: through the sphenoid ostium into the sphenoid sinus, then through the thin floor of the sella turcica. The sinus is well pneumatised under the sella in most adults (sellar type), but a small presellar or conchal sinus in children makes the approach harder.
The relations determine the hazards: the internal carotid arteries and cavernous sinuses lie on either side (carotid injury is the most feared complication, and tumour invading the cavernous sinus often cannot be removed completely), the optic chiasm and nerves lie above, and the sphenopalatine arteries lie at the front of the sinus (post-operative epistaxis). Other complications are CSF rhinorrhoea when the diaphragma sellae is breached, meningitis, diabetes insipidus and hypopituitarism, so cortisol cover and fluid balance are monitored. Sphenoid sinusitis can spread directly to the cavernous sinus and optic nerve.

title: Inferior petrosal sinus sampling in Cushing syndrome
text:
The pituitary drains into the cavernous sinuses and then through the inferior petrosal sinuses to the internal jugular veins. In ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome, MRI often fails to show a pituitary microadenoma (or shows an incidental one), and the alternative is ectopic ACTH from a small cell lung carcinoma or bronchial carcinoid.
Catheters placed in both inferior petrosal sinuses via the femoral veins sample ACTH simultaneously with a peripheral vein, before and after corticotropin-releasing hormone. A central-to-peripheral ACTH ratio of 2 or more at baseline, or 3 or more after CRH, localises the source to the pituitary (Cushing disease); a flat gradient indicates ectopic secretion. Lateralisation between the two sides is unreliable because of asymmetric venous drainage. Rare complications include brainstem venous injury and thrombosis.

title: Adrenal venous sampling and the adrenal incidentaloma
text:
Each adrenal has three arteries (superior from the inferior phrenic, middle from the aorta, inferior from the renal artery) but a single central vein. The right vein is very short and enters the posterior IVC; the left is longer and joins the left renal vein with the inferior phrenic vein.
In primary aldosteronism, CT cannot reliably distinguish a unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma (curable by adrenalectomy) from bilateral hyperplasia (treated with spironolactone), and non-functioning nodules are common. Adrenal venous sampling compares aldosterone-to-cortisol ratios from each adrenal vein; cortisol confirms correct catheter position. Cannulating the tiny right vein is the technical challenge.
Incidental adrenal masses are found on about 4% of abdominal CTs. Every one needs biochemical screening (overnight dexamethasone suppression for autonomous cortisol, plasma metanephrines for phaeochromocytoma, aldosterone-renin ratio if hypertensive) and imaging assessment: a small homogeneous lipid-rich lesion (low attenuation, under 10 HU) is a benign adenoma, whereas size over 4 cm or heterogeneous enhancement raises concern for carcinoma or metastasis.

title: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
text:
Autosomal recessive defects in cortisol synthesis, over 90% due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Low cortisol drives ACTH, the adrenals hypertrophy, and precursors are shunted into adrenal androgens; in the salt-wasting form aldosterone is also deficient.
Girls (46,XX) are born with virilised, ambiguous genitalia but normal internal female organs. Boys look normal and present at 1 to 3 weeks with a salt-wasting crisis: vomiting, dehydration, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and shock, which is why the first sign may be collapse. Milder forms cause early pubic hair, rapid growth with premature epiphyseal fusion (short adults), and hirsutism and irregular periods in women. A raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone confirms it. Treatment is lifelong hydrocortisone (with doubled 'sick-day' doses) and fludrocortisone. 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency causes virilisation with HYPERtension from deoxycorticosterone excess.

title: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours and the gastrinoma triangle
text:
Most gastrinomas lie within the gastrinoma (Passaro) triangle, bounded by the junction of the cystic and common bile ducts, the junction of the second and third parts of the duodenum, and the junction of the neck and body of the pancreas; many are small tumours in the duodenal wall. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome causes multiple, refractory or post-bulbar (jejunal) peptic ulcers with diarrhoea and a very high fasting gastrin despite gastric acid.
Other pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours: insulinoma (Whipple triad of fasting hypoglycaemia symptoms, glucose under 3.0 mmol/L and relief with glucose; high insulin AND C-peptide, whereas injected insulin suppresses C-peptide), glucagonoma (necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes, weight loss), VIPoma (watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, achlorhydria) and somatostatinoma (gallstones, diabetes, steatorrhoea).
About a quarter of gastrinomas occur in MEN1 (parathyroid hyperplasia, pituitary adenoma, pancreatic and duodenal tumours; menin gene), so calcium should always be checked.

title: Pancreas divisum and pancreatic duct anatomy
text:
The pancreas forms from dorsal and ventral buds. The ventral bud rotates behind the duodenum with the bile duct and forms the lower head and uncinate process; the main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung) forms from the ventral duct plus the distal dorsal duct and joins the bile duct at the major duodenal papilla (ampulla of Vater). The proximal dorsal duct persists as the accessory duct (of Santorini), draining through the minor papilla.
In pancreas divisum (about 7% of people) the ducts fail to fuse, so most of the gland drains through the small minor papilla; most people are asymptomatic but it may contribute to recurrent acute pancreatitis, treated by minor papilla sphincterotomy. A long common channel of the bile and pancreatic ducts explains gallstone pancreatitis and, when abnormally long, a pancreaticobiliary maljunction predisposing to choledochal cysts and gallbladder cancer. ERCP cannulates the major papilla, and post-ERCP pancreatitis is its commonest complication.

title: Processus vaginalis: hydrocele, indirect hernia and undescended testis
text:
The gubernaculum guides the testis from the posterior abdominal wall through the inguinal canal into the scrotum in the last trimester, preceded by a pouch of peritoneum, the processus vaginalis, which normally obliterates, leaving only the tunica vaginalis around the testis.
A widely patent processus gives an indirect inguinal hernia (the commonest hernia in children, especially premature boys; repaired promptly because of incarceration risk). A narrow patent processus admits only fluid: a communicating hydrocele that varies in size during the day. Non-communicating hydroceles in adults surround the testis, transilluminate and one can 'get above' them, unlike a hernia; a new hydrocele in a young man warrants ultrasound to exclude a testicular tumour.
Undescended testes (3% of term boys, commoner in premature) usually lie in the canal; those not descended by 3 months are fixed in the scrotum (orchidopexy) by 6-18 months to protect fertility and allow self-examination, although cancer risk remains raised. A retractile testis that can be brought down to the scrotum is normal.

title: Anal fissure, abscess and fistula
text:
Anal fissures are tears of the anoderm below the pectinate line, usually in the posterior midline (anterior after childbirth), where the blood supply is poorest; spasm of the internal sphincter maintains ischaemia. They cause severe pain on defecation with fresh bleeding on the paper. Topical glyceryl trinitrate or diltiazem relax the sphincter; botulinum toxin or lateral internal sphincterotomy treat chronic fissures. Lateral or multiple fissures suggest Crohn disease, HIV, syphilis, tuberculosis or carcinoma.
Most anorectal abscesses start in an infected anal gland at the dentate line and track into the perianal, ischioanal, intersphincteric or supralevator spaces; they need incision and drainage. About a third leave a fistula-in-ano. Goodsall rule: an external opening anterior to a transverse line through the anus usually leads straight to the nearest crypt, whereas a posterior opening follows a curved track to the posterior midline. High fistulas crossing much of the external sphincter are treated with a seton rather than laid open, to preserve continence.

title: Obstetric anal sphincter injury and faecal continence
text:
Continence depends on the internal anal sphincter (smooth muscle, resting tone), the external anal sphincter (skeletal, pudendal nerve, voluntary squeeze) and the puborectalis sling of levator ani, which pulls the anorectal junction forward to create an anorectal angle of about 90 degrees; the angle straightens during defecation.
Perineal tears in childbirth are graded: first degree skin; second degree perineal muscles; third degree the anal sphincter complex (3a less than half of the external sphincter, 3b more than half, 3c internal sphincter too); fourth degree the anal mucosa as well. Risk factors are forceps delivery, first birth, a large baby, occipitoposterior position, prolonged second stage and midline episiotomy. A mediolateral episiotomy cut at about 60 degrees from the midline reduces sphincter injury. Every tear must be examined rectally so that sphincter damage is recognised and repaired immediately; unrecognised injury is a leading cause of faecal incontinence in women, often presenting years later.

title: Obstetric pelvis: types, diameters and pelvic girdle pain
text:
The gynaecoid pelvis (about half of women) has a round inlet, wide subpubic arch and blunt ischial spines, favouring delivery. The android pelvis (heart-shaped inlet, prominent spines, narrow arch) predisposes to deep transverse arrest and occipitoposterior positions; the anthropoid pelvis (long anteroposterior axis) favours direct occipitoposterior delivery; the platypelloid pelvis (flat) delays engagement.
The obstetric conjugate, from the sacral promontory to the nearest point on the back of the pubic symphysis, is the narrowest inlet diameter (about 11 cm). The interspinous diameter between the ischial spines (about 10 cm) is the narrowest part of the midpelvis, and the station of the fetal head is measured in centimetres above or below the spines.
In pregnancy relaxin loosens the symphysis and sacroiliac joints, causing pelvic girdle pain (symphysis pubis dysfunction) with pain on walking, turning in bed and standing on one leg. A symphyseal gap of more than about 1 cm after delivery is a pathological diastasis.

title: Sacrospinous fixation and the sciatic foramina
text:
The sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments convert the sciatic notches into the greater and lesser sciatic foramina and resist upward rotation of the lower sacrum under body weight. Piriformis, the sciatic nerve, gluteal vessels and the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels leave through the greater foramen; the pudendal neurovascular bundle then crosses the back of the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament to enter the perineum through the lesser foramen.
In sacrospinous fixation for vaginal vault or uterine prolapse, the vault is sutured to the ligament through a vaginal approach. Sutures are placed about two centimetres medial to the ischial spine to avoid the pudendal nerve and vessels (buttock and perineal pain, haemorrhage) and the sciatic nerve above. The ligaments are also surgical landmarks in pelvic fracture fixation, and the sacrotuberous ligament is a site of pudendal nerve entrapment.

title: Obturator hernia and the obturator jerk
text:
The obturator canal, the gap at the top of the obturator membrane where the obturator nerve and vessels leave the pelvis, can admit a hernia, typically in thin elderly multiparous women ('little old lady's hernia'). It usually presents as small bowel obstruction, often a Richter hernia of part of the bowel wall, with no visible lump because it lies deep to pectineus. Compression of the obturator nerve causes pain down the medial thigh to the knee, worse with extension, adduction or internal rotation of the hip (Howship-Romberg sign). CT is diagnostic, and delayed diagnosis carries high mortality.
During transurethral resection of tumours on the lateral bladder wall, electrical stimulation of the obturator nerve lying just outside can cause a violent adductor jerk and bladder perforation; an obturator nerve block or muscle relaxation prevents it. The nerve is also dissected along the pelvic side wall in pelvic lymphadenectomy.

title: Neurogenic bladder by level of lesion
text:
Parasympathetic fibres from S2-S4 (pelvic splanchnic nerves) contract the detrusor. Sympathetic fibres from T11-L2 (hypogastric nerves) relax the detrusor and close the bladder neck, which also prevents retrograde ejaculation. Somatic pudendal fibres from Onuf nucleus (S2-S4) control the external urethral sphincter. The pontine micturition centre coordinates detrusor contraction with sphincter relaxation, under frontal lobe inhibition.
Suprapontine lesions (stroke, dementia, normal pressure hydrocephalus, frontal tumours) cause an overactive bladder: urgency and urge incontinence with coordinated, complete emptying. Spinal cord lesions between the pons and sacral cord (trauma, multiple sclerosis) cause detrusor overactivity with detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia: high bladder pressures, incomplete emptying, reflux, hydronephrosis and renal failure unless pressures are controlled (intermittent catheterisation, antimuscarinics, botulinum toxin). Sacral cord, cauda equina or pelvic nerve lesions (cauda equina syndrome, diabetes, radical pelvic surgery) cause an atonic, insensate bladder with painless retention and overflow incontinence.

title: Erection, ejaculation and nerve-sparing pelvic surgery
text:
'Point, squeeze and shoot': erection is parasympathetic (S2-S4 cavernous nerves releasing nitric oxide, which relaxes the smooth muscle of the cavernosal arteries and sinusoids so they fill and compress the draining veins); emission of semen into the posterior urethra is sympathetic (T11-L2); ejaculation is rhythmic contraction of bulbospongiosus and the pelvic floor via the pudendal nerve.
The cavernous nerves run in the neurovascular bundles along the posterolateral surface of the prostate, so radical prostatectomy, cystectomy and low rectal cancer surgery can cause erectile dysfunction; nerve-sparing techniques dissect the bundles off the prostatic capsule when the cancer allows. Post-prostatectomy stress incontinence reflects reliance on the external urethral sphincter once the bladder neck and prostatic urethra are removed. Retroperitoneal lymph node dissection for testicular cancer can damage the lumbar sympathetic chain and hypogastric plexus, causing failure of emission or retrograde ejaculation, prevented by nerve-sparing templates. Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors potentiate nitric oxide and need intact nerves to work well.

title: Pelvic lymph node dissection in urological and gynaecological cancer
text:
Pelvic node dissection clears the tissue around the external iliac vessels, the obturator fossa (bounded by the external iliac vein, the pelvic side wall and the obturator nerve, which is identified and preserved) and the internal iliac vessels, sometimes up to the common iliac bifurcation.
The prostate drains mainly to the obturator and internal iliac nodes, then the common iliac and para-aortic nodes; the bladder to the external and internal iliac nodes; the cervix to the parametrial, obturator and internal iliac nodes; the penis and vulva first to the superficial inguinal nodes, then the deep inguinal nodes (the highest, Cloquet node, lies in the femoral canal) and only then to the pelvis. Node status is central to staging and to whether pelvic radiotherapy is added.
Complications include obturator nerve injury (adductor weakness), external iliac vein injury, lymphocele (a lymph collection that can compress the bladder or iliac vein and cause DVT) and lower limb or genital lymphoedema, especially when combined with radiotherapy.

title: Pelviureteric junction obstruction
text:
The pelviureteric junction is the first of the three natural narrowings of the ureter (with the pelvic brim, where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels, and the vesicoureteric junction) and is where stones often lodge. Congenital pelviureteric junction obstruction, from an aperistaltic segment of ureter, a high insertion or a lower-pole crossing vessel, is the commonest cause of antenatally detected hydronephrosis and of an abdominal mass in neonates.
In older children and adults it presents with intermittent loin pain after a large fluid load (classically beer drinking, Dietl crisis), infection or stones. Ultrasound shows a dilated renal pelvis and calyces with a normal ureter; a MAG3 diuretic renogram measures split function and drainage. Pyeloplasty (Anderson-Hynes dismembered pyeloplasty, often laparoscopic or robotic) excises the narrowed segment and transposes the ureter in front of any crossing vessel.

title: Posterior urethral valves and vesicoureteric reflux
text:
Posterior urethral valves are obstructing mucosal folds in the prostatic urethra of boys, the commonest cause of bladder outlet obstruction in male infants. Antenatal ultrasound shows bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, a thick-walled distended bladder with a dilated posterior urethra (the 'keyhole' sign) and oligohydramnios, which causes pulmonary hypoplasia and Potter sequence (flat facies, limb deformities). After birth there is a poor urinary stream, a palpable bladder, infection and renal impairment; a micturating cystourethrogram is diagnostic and the valves are ablated endoscopically. Many boys still progress to chronic kidney disease.
Vesicoureteric reflux results from a short intramural (submucosal) course of the ureter through the bladder wall, which normally acts as a flap valve. It causes recurrent febrile urinary tract infections and renal scarring (reflux nephropathy, hypertension). It is graded I to V on micturating cystourethrography; low grades often resolve as the tunnel lengthens with growth, while high grades may need antibiotic prophylaxis, endoscopic injection or ureteric reimplantation.

title: Obstructive azoospermia
text:
The seminal vesicles contribute most of the ejaculate volume and its fructose and alkaline fluid; their ducts join the ductus deferens to form the ejaculatory ducts, which open on the verumontanum of the prostatic urethra.
Obstruction of the ejaculatory ducts (congenital cysts, post-inflammatory scarring, calculi) produces a characteristic semen analysis: low volume (under about 1.5 mL), acidic, azoospermic and fructose-negative, with normal testicular size and hormones. Transrectal ultrasound shows dilated seminal vesicles or a midline cyst, and transurethral resection of the ejaculatory ducts can restore flow.
Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens gives a similar picture and is a mild form of cystic fibrosis (CFTR mutations), so the couple should have genetic testing before sperm retrieval and IVF. Normal-volume azoospermia with small soft testes and a high FSH points instead to testicular (non-obstructive) failure such as Klinefelter syndrome.
